narrative: Ticket volume is high and touches nearly every module, but each individual fault gets fixed within 1-2 days and the account keeps engaging normally in between. The exception is exports, which fails three separate ways (blank, wrong data, broken) across the year, prompting the final ticket to ask support to "look at the underlying issue instead of firefighting each one" rather than accept another quick patch. That's a specific, actionable signal that the export module needs a root-cause fix, not evidence the relationship itself is at risk.

Four unrelated failures pile up between January and May (dashboards, seat provisioning, report builder, exports), culminating in an explicit request for a call to understand "what's actually going on," then an August API outage where the customer notes they'd have expected "a dedicated point of contact" by now. September brings genuine payoff: the dashboard fix is confirmed as having "actually solved" the January issue, the API fix is credited to an engineer who "walked us through the token refresh setup directly," and the remaining tickets are calm feature requests and thanks. This is anger and escalation followed by real resolution.

Three routine, well-spaced tickets over a year: a seat/billing sync question, an export-formatting workflow question, and a holiday-scheduling check. No complaints, no repeat problems, nothing suggesting friction with the product.

Ingrid and Tuomas document every issue meticulously and specifically call out that the November export-queuing problem was "never properly resolved — the jobs eventually ran but we got no explanation" before failing a third time in December. By January, dashboard load-time degradation gets six weeks of self-collected data and is flagged as "a genuine operational concern," and by March the account is submitting tickets just to get things confirmed rather than trusting they work: "I prefer not to assume things work until confirmed." This is the quiet, well-documented erosion pattern rather than loud complaint.

competitor_mentions.quote: we did look briefly at Storsund BI during the CRM transition since we were reviewing several vendor relationships at once, but decided to stick with Kataja for now

narrative: Light, practical traffic: a naming-convention request, a CRM connector migration during which they mention having glanced at a competitor before deciding to stay, and a tidy-up seat request. The competitor mention is incidental to a decision already made in Kataja's favour, not a live evaluation.

The Salesforce connector auth failure recurs at least five times across a year with escalating sarcasm — "we're doing your reauth job for you," "I feel like I send this exact ticket every quarter" — and is never actually fixed, only re-authorised each time. The same pattern repeats for a stale-data dashboard widget (three tickets in four days demanding it be escalated "to whoever actually owns this") and for duplicate alert emails, still unresolved at the final ticket ("please confirm the fix actually went out on our instance"). High ticket volume here reflects genuinely unfixed recurring defects, not just an engaged complainer.

competitor_mentions.quote: Dashlume's Enterprise pricing model came up for comparison during a recent budget conversation, so it would help to understand ours clearly either way

narrative: A careful, low-volume account: a considered dashboard-access rollout in August, a minor email-deliverability question, and a billing clarification. The January ticket is the one to watch: a permissions bug (a regional lead seeing another region's figures) sat undetected since August, was caught only during a close review, and is now handled with a manual stopgap while the customer asks for "confidence this is properly fixed rather than patched again." No anger, but a real cross-region access-control failure that took five months to surface.

Three short, unambiguously positive tickets: a smooth bulk seat setup, a webhook request turned around same day ("impressive"), and a scheduling change handled without having to chase. A healthy, low-maintenance account.

Six tickets over the year, all feature requests or minor bugs met with real fixes or workable workarounds, and later tickets confirm earlier fixes are holding ("running smoothly now that we've tuned the window"). An engaged, satisfied user of the product, not a source of concern.

competitor_mentions.quote: Looked at Dashlume during our renewal review mainly for the role-based visibility feature, but since you shipped that a couple of months ago there wasn't much reason to switch

narrative: An expanding account: replacing an Excel pack, building a second dashboard, adding read-only API access for an auditor, with every request resolved well. The one competitor mention is the best kind of news: a genuine renewal-time evaluation of Dashlume that ended with the customer staying because Kataja shipped the feature they needed. Growing usage plus a resolved competitive threat points to a secure relationship.
Two straightforward tickets eight weeks apart: a seat-count clarification ahead of renewal and an SSO/SAML setup question, both resolved without complaint. No signal of friction.

This account files tickets almost weekly across every module for over a year, and a meaningful share are genuine repeats: dashboard slow-load returns a month after being "fixed" ("did the fix actually ship, or did it regress?"), alert thresholds reset three times, and alerts that were just fixed start firing twice. The final week (early September 2025) is the clearest sign of unresolved rot: the same export date-range bug is reported three times in six days with no indication it actually stuck. High volume here is a symptom of things not staying fixed.

Pekka's tickets are detailed and professional throughout, but the arc is concerning: genuine anger in December ("I should not have to submit a third ticket to get a response on something this fundamental") and January ("increasingly difficult to explain to my colleagues why basic functions are not working") gives way not to resolution but to resignation. By March he is pre-emptively building his own workarounds and asking support to look into things "when you get a chance" with "a workaround in place for now." The API rate-limit question raised in July is still unresolved by October and never gets a follow-up confirming a fix. This is disengagement dressed as patience, not improvement.

competitor_mentions.quote: We're finalizing our reporting stack after comparing Kataja against Storsund BI, and this export format mismatch needs sorting before we can commit fully
One thing that came up again while we compare notes against Storsund BI - we can't filter a dashboard by a custom date range, only preset periods.
Sat through a Dashlume demo last week as part of a routine vendor review - their alert builder looked a bit more flexible.
Dashlume apparently offers that, curious if it's on your side too.

narrative: This account benchmarks against competitors repeatedly and openly, Storsund BI during an active vendor decision in 2024, then Dashlume during "a routine vendor review" in mid-2025, and each time explicitly says they're staying with Kataja. The one open thread worth watching is a custom-date-range dashboard filter, requested in 2024, marked unresolved, and never followed up on: exactly the kind of small recurring gap that keeps a competitor's name in the room even after a renewal decision.

A quiet account (four tickets in a year) with one loose end: an alert configured to catch sales drops was reported as unreliable in September 2024 ("worked twice, missed twice") and the account never files a follow-up confirming it was fixed, simply moving on to a connector setup and a seat transfer. Not dramatic, but a live monitoring gap with no evidence it was closed.

A genuinely bad first eight months: a connector failure from August 2024 recurs twice more without being picked up for days, seat provisioning breaks on top of it, and by April 2025 the customer explicitly requests escalation to "someone senior on your side reviewing the whole history." What follows is real recovery: August tickets confirm the dashboard fix held for two weeks of daily checking, the connector has been "solid... first real stretch without an issue since last August," and alerts are stable too. This is the anger-to-genuine-resolution arc working as intended.

Almost every module in this account has its own recurring, never-actually-fixed bug: the formula-save error in report builder returns at least four times over nine months ("I've genuinely lost count of how many times I've reported this"), alert rules vanish repeatedly ("this happens every couple of months now"), and a password-reset bug from March reappears in August with the customer asking to "fix it properly this time instead of a workaround." By October the customer states outright that "every module has its own recurring bug at this point." No ticket in the whole history confirms a fix actually held.
Three tickets over six months, all expansion-driven (new department seats, a tighter permission group, a new HR-system connector) and all resolved without complaint. A growing, low-friction account.

Sparse, practical traffic: a missing export column, a read-only dashboard-sharing request, an alert recipient-list question, and an early flag for a year-end export customisation. Nothing recurs and nothing is left hanging.

competitor_mentions.quote: We had a brief look at Dashlume last year during a vendor refresh and nothing came of it then, but this kind of knock-on effect is the sort of thing that would bring it back into the conversation

narrative: Three cascading problems in a single fortnight: a new ERP connector goes live, then an unrelated-seeming API integration starts throwing intermittent 500s, then an alert fires on stale data from the same new connector. The customer explicitly distrusts the new connector as a result: "we'll hold off adding any further data sources through it for now and stick to manual checks." Tying that reliability concern directly to the possibility of bringing Dashlume "back into the conversation" is a real warning shot, even though the tone stays measured throughout.
